sections.title: BACKGROUND

summary.text: Describes the background to the policy brief, noting progress in preventing vertical HIV transmission but missed targets, with an estimated 85% of pregnant women living with HIV on treatment and 150 000 infants acquiring HIV in 2020. It stresses the need to reduce transmission risk and to support child survival, growth and development.

sections.extract: of HIV, the targets for maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage and new vertical transmission have yet to be achieved (1). Globally, an estimated 85% of pregnant women living with HIV were receiving lifelong ART, and 150 000 infants acquired HIV through vertical transmission in 2020. Although more than 84% of vertical tranmissions occur in sub-Saharan Africa, it is encouraging that eastern and southern Africa

sections.title: Justification for the comprehensive package of care for infants and young children exposed to HIV

summary.text: Justifies a comprehensive package of care by citing high losses of mothers and HIV-exposed infants between antenatal care, delivery, early testing and final diagnosis. It argues that an integrated package eases navigation for mothers and children and improves access to services for HIV-free survival.

sections.extract: of care for infants and young children exposed to HIV A systematic review revealed that 49% of women living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa are lost between antenatal care registration and delivery, 34% of infants exposed to HIV are lost to follow-up by three months and a further 45% of infants exposed to HIV are lost after their first HIV test and before definitive diagnosis (13). sections.title: Overview of the interventions along the continuum of care

summary.text: Notes that children under two routinely receive well-child services such as immunization, growth monitoring and feeding counselling, and that HIV-exposed infants also need a specific package of care.

sections.extract: the continuum of care Children younger than two years typically receive well- child visits for routine services, including immunization, monitoring growth and development, micronutrient supplementation, deworming, preventing and managing common childhood conditions as well as infant feeding counselling and support. sections.title: Components of the comprehensive package of care for infants and young children exposed to HIV

summary.text: Lists the maternal and infant components of the comprehensive package of care, from maternal HIV testing, treatment and monitoring to infant diagnosis, antiretroviral and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, postnatal care, infant feeding and nurturing care.

sections.extract: of care for infants and young children exposed to HIV The comprehensive package of care brings together interventions across the continuum of care that collectively aim to reduce the risk of vertical transmission of HIV and improve the health and well-being of infants and young children exposed to HIV. The package includes both maternal and infant components (Fig. 1): • maternal HIV testing and retesting: other

sections.title: Scope

summary.text: Defines the scope of the policy brief as care for HIV-exposed infants and young children up to two years, with emphasis on maternal interventions that shape decisions about infant care. It excludes a full service package for children living with HIV.

sections.extract: Although the comprehensive package of care includes maternal, infant and young child interventions, this policy brief focuses mainly on the service package for infants and young children up to two years of age who are exposed to HIV. It emphasizes the maternal interventions that directly affect decision-making for interventions for the infants and young children exposed to HIV. For the detailed interventions for

sections.title: Maternal HIV testing and retesting

summary.text: Stresses early HIV testing in pregnancy with same-day ART for women who test positive, and retesting and partner testing for those at risk. It recommends third-trimester retesting for women of unknown or HIV-negative status in high-burden settings.

sections.extract: Preventing unplanned pregnancy and HIV acquisition, confirming HIV status before pregnancy, early identification of HIV infection during pregnancy and breastfeeding and timely initiation of ART are critical for minimizing vertical HIV transmission. All pregnant women should be offered HIV testing at the earliest opportunity during pregnancy and, if HIV positive, same- day initiation of ART. HIV re-testing and

summary.text: Describes HIV retesting in high-burden settings and risk-based retesting in low-burden settings, including an optional postpartum retest for women at elevated risk. It notes that suggested timings coincide with health service contacts and should prioritize high-incidence areas and key populations.

sections.extract: settings, retesting should be based on risk, emphasizing the need for ongoing risk screening (Box 2). summary.text: Gives the guidance for low-burden settings on retesting pregnant women at ongoing risk in late pregnancy, catch-up testing when tests are missed and optional postpartum retesting for key populations.

sections.extract: Retest pregnant women with unknown or HIV-negative status who are in serodiscordant relationships, whose partner does not have suppressed viral loads on ART or who have other known ongoing HIV risk in late pregnancy – at a third-trimester visit. sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Lists strategies to identify maternal HIV earlier by promoting early and complete antenatal care and facility births, including woman-held case notes and midwife-led continuity of care. It suggests high-prevalence countries consider routine postnatal retesting for all women.

sections.extract: Strategies to improve early identification of maternal HIV infection should include activities that promote early initiation of antenatal services, attending all recommended antenatal visits and promoting facility deliveries. sections.title: Viral load monitoring

summary.text: Recommends viral load monitoring during pregnancy and breastfeeding to identify women who need help achieving viral suppression, and summarizes WHO's routine monitoring schedule. It introduces a table on monitoring treatment for pregnant and breastfeeding women.

sections.extract: Viral load monitoring during pregnancy and the breastfeeding period is recommended to identify women who already have suppressed viral loads and to offer timely intervention to achieve viral suppression in women who are viraemic during the period of HIV transmission risk. The 2021 WHO consolidated guidelines (2) recommend routine viral load monitoring at six and 12 months after initiating ART and every 12 months

summary.text: A table of actions for viral load testing in pregnant women, depending on whether they started ART before or during pregnancy, including following the monitoring algorithm and considering infant testing at birth.

sections.title: Point-of-care viral load testing

summary.text: Sets out evidence that point-of-care viral load testing improves access, speeds results and helps continuity of treatment, and recommends prioritizing it for pregnant and breastfeeding women. It lists requirements such as quality assurance, supply chains and maintenance.

sections.extract: Evidence suggests that point-of-care viral load testing has the capacity to improve access to viral load testing, reduce turnaround time for results to the clinician, increase the probability of same-day results, improve the timeliness of clinical action to address elevated viral load and increase continuity of treatment and viral suppression (30–32). sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Recommends expanding viral load testing through laboratory capacity, sample transport, dried blood spot collection and point-of-care networks. It then describes the early infant diagnosis schedule, including testing at six weeks, after breastfeeding exposure and serology at 18 months.

sections.extract: Viral load testing capacity and coverage should be expanded by scaling up laboratory viral load testing infrastructure; strengthening the efficiency of sample processing and transport systems; supporting community viral load sample collection and testing using dried blood spot or plasma separation card and establishing networks for point-of-care viral load testing to improve access on the maternal; newborn and child

sections.title: Early infant diagnosis for high-risk infants

summary.text: Suggests that high-risk infants may be offered nucleic acid testing at birth, and that infants first found to be exposed after delivery should be tested and started on presumptive treatment.

sections.extract: Nucleic acid testing at birth may be considered for high- risk infants. In addition, infants who are first identified as HIV-exposed postpartum have a high cumulative risk of already having acquired HIV by the time prophylaxis is initiated. Under these circumstances, HIV nucleic acid testing should be performed and presumptive treatment started to avoid extended prophylaxis among infants who are already HIV infected

sections.title: Point-of-care infant diagnosis

summary.text: Reports that only 60% of HIV-exposed infants were tested by two months of age in 2020, with delays in results and linkage to treatment. It describes evidence that point-of-care nucleic acid testing speeds results and treatment and calls for systematic follow-up of mother–baby pairs.

sections.extract: Access to early infant diagnosis remains low, with only 60% of infants exposed to HIV globally tested by the second month of age in 2020 (39). Even when infants are tested, delays in receiving test results and weak linkage to ART contribute to attrition along the testing- to-treatment cascade. Evidence suggests that point-of- care nucleic acid testing enables more rapid testing with return of results to caregivers

sections.title: INFANT DIAGNOSIS

summary.text: Presents WHO's strong recommendation to use point-of-care nucleic acid testing to diagnose HIV in children under 18 months, with guidance on placing these technologies. It also covers infant feeding, noting that mothers on ART with suppressed viral loads can breastfeed up to two years.

sections.title: INFANT ANTIRETROVIRAL PROPHYLAXIS

summary.text: Presents a WHO good practice statement that ART should start before or urgently during pregnancy and breastfeeding, since suppressing maternal viral load is the most effective way to prevent vertical transmission.

sections.extract: Box 5. WHO good practice statement ART should be initiated before pregnancy and urgently among all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, even if they are identified late in pregnancy or postpartum, because the most effective way to reduce the risk of HIV vertical transmission is to suppress maternal viral load. Whenever possible, all efforts should be made to identify HIV-infected pregnant women early

sections.title: Risk assessment of infants exposed to HIV

summary.text: Explains how HIV-exposed infants are assessed as low or high risk of vertical transmission based on maternal treatment and viral load. Infants are low risk when mothers are on ART with suppressed viral loads, and WHO's definition of high-risk infants is given.

sections.extract: Risk assessment is based on prevailing maternal factors that affect the probability of HIV vertical transmission and is essential for selecting appropriate preventive interventions for infants exposed to HIV. Infants exposed to HIV are considered to have low risk for vertical transmission if their mothers are receiving ART and have suppressed viral loads during pregnancy and delivery and throughout breastfeeding.

sections.title: Antiretroviral prophylaxis

summary.text: States that a single antiretroviral drug for four to six weeks is recommended as postnatal prophylaxis for infants at low risk of vertical transmission.

sections.extract: Infants at low risk of vertical transmission should receive a single ARV drug as postnatal prophylaxis for 4–6 weeks (Box 6).

sections.title: Enhanced postnatal prophylaxis

summary.text: Describes enhanced postnatal prophylaxis for high-risk infants using dual antiretroviral drugs for six weeks followed by six more weeks of dual or single drugs, with alternative regimens if needed. It gives the related WHO recommendation and its certainty of evidence.

sections.extract: Infants at high risk for vertical transmission should receive dual ARV drugs for six weeks followed by dual or single ARV drugs for another six weeks for a total of 12 weeks (Box 6). When the recommended regimen is not available or feasible, alternative options such as RAL, 3TC, LPV/r solid formulations or triple-drug fixed-dose combinations containing AZT, NVP and 3TC may be considered (see Annex 1 for the dosing

sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Reports how 18 priority countries have adopted enhanced postnatal prophylaxis, some for all breastfeeding HIV-exposed infants and others only for high-risk infants. It advises providing infant prophylaxis in the same setting as maternal ART.

sections.extract: Various countries have adopted enhanced postnatal prophylaxis using a variety of approaches to adapt to the country context. A policy review conducted in 18 AIDS Free priority countries revealed that seven countries adopted enhanced postnatal prophylaxis for all breastfeeding infants exposed to HIV and 11 countries for only high-risk infants. sections.title: Providing enhanced postnatal prophylaxis to all infants exposed to HIV

summary.text: Describes giving enhanced prophylaxis to all HIV-exposed infants as an interim measure where maternal ART and viral suppression are poor, noting the trade-offs of cost, drug supply and unnecessary toxicity.

sections.extract: exposed to HIV This may be considered in settings in which most mothers are at high risk of transmitting HIV because of poor maternal ART coverage, high rates of loss to follow-up, poor maternal viral load testing coverage and poor maternal viral suppression rates. It should serve as an interim measure as strategies to improve maternal ART coverage, maternal viral load testing coverage and maternal viral suppression

summary.text: Discusses extended prophylaxis beyond 12 weeks for infants still at high risk during breastfeeding, listing circumstances of persistent risk. It advises against restarting prophylaxis once stopped and favours support for maternal adherence instead.

sections.extract: 12 weeks Although limited evidence suggests additional benefit of combination or prolonged regimens in the context of maternal ART (44), infants and young children who remain at high risk for HIV transmission during the breastfeeding period may receive extended prophylaxis until the risk is considered limited or has ended. sections.title: Presumptive treatment

summary.text: Describes presumptive treatment for infants identified as HIV-exposed late, whose mothers were diagnosed late or infected while breastfeeding, involving nucleic acid testing and starting treatment straight away. It notes how the regimen should be adjusted after results.

sections.extract: Infants may be identified as exposed to HIV late when they present for health services outside the prevention- of-vertical-transmission cascade. Their mothers may be diagnosed with HIV late or may have acquired HIV during the breastfeeding period. These infants are at high risk of vertical transmission because of high levels of maternal viraemia and the absence of maternal ART. Under these circumstances, nucleic

sections.title: CO-TRIMOXAZOLE PROPHYLAXIS

summary.text: Describes the history of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in WHO guidelines since 2006, from preventing Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis to preventing malaria and severe bacterial infections. It presents the current recommendation for HIV-exposed infants and children.

sections.extract: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis was first introduced in the WHO guidelines in 2006 as a component of standard HIV care, primarily as prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis for people living with HIV and infants exposed to HIV until it could be reliably established that they were HIV-uninfected (46). In subsequent years, the use of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis was extended to preventing malaria

summary.text: States that co-trimoxazole should start for all HIV-exposed infants at four to six weeks and continue until HIV is excluded, as part of a table of initiation and discontinuation criteria.

sections.title: Infants exposed to HIV and uninfected

summary.text: Reviews evidence on co-trimoxazole for infants who are HIV-exposed but uninfected, citing trials that found no clear benefit, and discusses how policies might be applied in different settings. It then turns to health and development, noting that HIV-exposed children are more likely to have motor and cognitive delays. It introduces nurturing care, including health, nutrition, security, responsive caregiving and early learning.

sections.extract: A systematic review was conducted to assess the effect of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis on the morbidity and mortality of infants who are HIV exposed and uninfected (51). Two trials were identified that addressed the research question. A randomized placebo-controlled trial in Botswana (52) that started co-trimoxazole at 14–34 days and continued it until 15 months of age showed no evidence of benefit of co-trimoxazole

sections.title: PROMOTING NURTURING CARE

summary.text: Describes developmental assessments using standardized, validated tools to measure motor, cognitive, communication and social skills. It presents WHO's recommendation that all infants receive responsive care in their first three years.

sections.extract: Developmental assessments by direct measurement and observation are used to assess various aspects of a child’s functioning and abilities (motor, sensory, cognition, communication, behaviour, social interaction and adaptive skills). Systematic and structured developmental assessments using standardized validated tools are advised. Several age-dependent tools are used for formal developmental assessment, including

sections.title: Promote early learning

summary.text: States WHO's strong recommendation that all young children take part in early learning activities with caregivers during the first three years, with caregivers supported to do so.

sections.extract: All infants and children should have early learning activities with their parents and other caregivers during the first three years of life; parents and other caregivers should be supported to engage in early learning with their infants and children (strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence).

sections.title: Integrate caregiving and nutrition interventions

summary.text: States WHO's recommendation to include support for responsive care and early learning in infant and young child nutrition interventions.

sections.extract: Support for responsive care and early learning should be included as part of interventions for optimal nutrition of infants and young children (strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence).

sections.title: Support maternal mental health

summary.text: States WHO's recommendation to integrate psychosocial support for maternal mental health into early childhood health and development services.

sections.extract: Psychosocial interventions to support maternal mental health should be integrated into early childhood health and development services (strong recommendation; moderate-quality evidence). Source: Improving early childhood development (60).

sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Calls for multistakeholder and multisectoral approaches to nurturing care, locally validated developmental screening tools and referral systems for infants exposed to HIV.

sections.extract: Multistakeholder engagement and multisectoral approaches at the national and community levels to ensure local contexts and available supportive systems to implement nurturing care interventions are considered critical to comprehensive service delivery, uptake and sustainability. sections.title: POLICY IMPLEMENTATION CONSIDERATIONS FOR THE COMPREHENSIVE PACKAGE OF CARE

summary.text: Advises countries to adapt the comprehensive package of care to their capacity while still delivering all components together.

sections.extract: to their specific contexts based on the level of implementation and capacities for the individual components, nevertheless endeavouring to ensure that all the components of care are optimally delivered jointly in a comprehensive approach.

sections.title: National level

summary.text: Recommends placing the package of care for HIV-exposed infants on reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health platforms, aligned with related policies and backed by commodities, funding and coordination.

sections.extract: The comprehensive integrated package of care for infants and young children exposed to HIV should be strategically positioned on reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health platforms. Contextual assessment and inclusive multistakeholder engagement for operationalizing this package of care will be critical. sections.extract: The potential challenges of introducing a new care package within contexts of limited human resources and capacity at the different levels of care need to be carefully considered. summary.text: Continues the human resources point, listing tasks such as psychosocial and adherence support, sample transport and drug distribution that could be shared, with capacity building and innovative tools. It then describes service delivery, recommending integration of the care package into reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health platforms, with standard procedures and synchronized appointments for mother–infant pairs. It also calls for community-based strategies to keep exposed infants in care through to final diagnosis and to maintain services during disasters and pandemics.

sections.title: Monitoring, evaluation and learning

summary.text: Lists monitoring priorities for the care package for HIV-exposed infants, from antenatal and postnatal attendance and maternal ART and viral suppression to early infant diagnosis coverage and follow-up to final diagnosis. It also calls for implementation research to guide phased roll-out and for adequate funding and training of monitoring and evaluation staff.

sections.extract: Determining priorities for monitoring and evaluating the comprehensive package of care and identifying programme indicators are important for programmes. Priorities for monitoring will include: • antenatal initiation and attendance; • postnatal attendance; • the number of pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV disaggregated for timing of HIV diagnosis, maternal ART coverage, maternal ART timing, maternal

sections.title: Quality improvement

summary.text: Describes using quality improvement methods, quality indicators and client-led initiatives involving mothers to close gaps in care for HIV-exposed infants, particularly in decentralized, resource-limited settings.

sections.extract: To ensure a safe, effective, patient-centred comprehensive package of care for infants and young children who are HIV exposed, quality improvement can be used to address gaps along the continuum of care. Quality can be assessed to ensure that the standards of care are met and to minimize missed opportunities. Key to this will be identifying quality indicators. Quality improvement teams and/or health-care providers

sections.title: ARV drug prophylaxis

summary.text: Identifies research gaps on antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV-exposed infants, including the added value of combination or prolonged prophylaxis and prophylaxis when exposure is identified late or the mother acquires HIV after pregnancy begins. It also calls for better infant drug formulations and studies on maternal viraemia during breastfeeding and on defining high-risk infants.

sections.extract: The additional benefit of combination or prolonged infant prophylaxis with maternal ART remains uncertain. In addition, limited evidence supports infant prophylaxis for infants with HIV exposure identified during the postpartum period or the mother acquiring HIV during pregnancy and the breastfeeding period. Research is needed, including clinical and pharmacological studies, to inform the development of improved ARV

sections.title: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis

summary.text: States that WHO expects to fully review its co-trimoxazole prophylaxis recommendation for HIV-exposed infants as evidence accumulates. It lists research questions such as optimal start timing, shorter duration, alternative antibiotics, antimicrobial resistance and effects on the microbiome.

sections.extract: WHO anticipates fully reviewing the co-trimoxazole prophylaxis recommendation as further evidence is gathered and increasing progress is made, to rapidly identify infants living with HIV and retaining those exposed to HIV in the testing cascade until final diagnosis is ascertained. Research gaps remain about how to optimize the use of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and well-conducted operational research will be

sections.title: Other gaps

summary.text: Notes further research needs on integrating nurturing care and caregiver support into services for HIV-exposed infants and on the impact of HIV services integrated into routine child health care.

sections.extract: The impact of integrating nurturing care interventions into service delivery for infants and young children exposed to HIV needs to be better understood. The impact of caregiver support interventions may also need to be further explored. Finally, more research on integrated services is needed, especially to document the impact of HIV services when integrated into routine child services.
